profile.address: 4710, West Circle Drive Northwest, Rochester, Olmsted County, Minnesota, 55901
profile.reading:
This building at 4710 West Circle Drive Northwest in Rochester, Minnesota has a more layered ownership history than its "Epic / Mayo" registry name alone suggests. Mayo Clinic, the Rochester-headquartered nonprofit medical group founded from William Worrall Mayo's 1864 practice, originally built the facility in 2012 at a reported cost of about $33.7 million as its own data center supporting clinical and administrative systems across its Rochester, Minnesota; Jacksonville, Florida; and Phoenix/Scottsdale, Arizona campuses. In October 2015, Epic Systems -- the Verona, Wisconsin-based electronic health records company that supplies Mayo's clinical software and today handles a large share of the nation's electronic patient records -- announced it would acquire the building, and completed the purchase on December 29, 2015 for $46 million. The deal was structured as a sale-leaseback: Epic took ownership and operation of the roughly 62,000-square-foot facility while leasing space back to Mayo Clinic under an open-ended arrangement running a minimum of four years. The timing coincided with Mayo's move to consolidate multiple legacy electronic-record systems onto a single Epic platform, implemented in 2017, and with a broader Mayo-Epic-IBM Watson Health collaboration exploring cognitive-computing tools for matching patients to clinical trials. Epic reportedly planned to staff the site with 80-90 employees and discussed potential capacity expansion to as much as three times the building's original size. Local reporting in the years since confirms continued capital investment in the site: a nearly $4 million mechanical and electrical upgrade was reported for the facility (described in that coverage as having grown to roughly 77,000 square feet), and Epic worked with Rochester Public Utilities to build a dedicated $6.1 million electrical substation to support the site's power demands, indicating a load significant enough to warrant utility-side infrastructure rather than a standard commercial service tap. Neither Epic nor Mayo Clinic publishes a current IT-load, cooling-design, or uptime-certification figure for the building, consistent with its role as a mission-specific healthcare-data facility rather than a commercially marketed colocation site; its public specification, in effect, is measured in mechanical-upgrade permits and utility investment rather than a marketing spec sheet.

The arrangement is a useful illustration of how large software vendors have moved beyond selling licenses to owning physical infrastructure that keeps a marquee customer's systems running, and it means that although the public commonly hears the site described in relation to Mayo Clinic, the entity actually responsible for its day-to-day operation, staffing, and capital upgrades since 2015 has been Epic Systems.

reading.body:
This facility is a roughly 77,000-square-foot data center in Rochester, Minnesota, built by Mayo Clinic in 2012 and purchased by Epic Systems in a sale-leaseback in December 2015. Epic has operated the site since then with 80-90 of its own staff, hosting Mayo's electronic health records systems across Mayo's three major U.S. campuses. The building does not publish an IT load, cooling design, or uptime specification, which is consistent with its role as mission-critical healthcare infrastructure rather than a commercial colocation product.

The scale of the facility is indicated by infrastructure investment rather than published capacity. In 2019, Epic completed a nearly $4 million mechanical and electrical upgrade, and it worked with Rochester Public Utilities to construct a dedicated $6.1 million electrical substation to support the site's power demands, implying that standard commercial service was insufficient for the load. This level of utility-side capital investment suggests the data center operates at a scale material enough to warrant dedicated grid infrastructure, though the exact megawatt figure remains unpublished.

Minnesota's published data center capacity totals 10 MW across only two facilities with disclosed figures; this campus does not disclose its capacity and ranks third in the state by published megawatts. The 13 mapped facilities in Minnesota represent a thin registry, and the vast majority publish no specification at all. This facility's absence from published capacity figures reflects its design as proprietary healthcare infrastructure for a single operator rather than a commercially marketed resource, and its actual power draw remains opaque to the public record.
